All confined space rescues must be performed by the local fire department.
The plan violates ANSI Z359, which prohibits vertical entry rescues.
feedbacks: Incorrect: A CP can write the plan, but it must be adequate and incorporate all hazards.

Correct: Rescue planning under 1926.502(d)(20) must account for the specific work environment. A fall into a PRCS is a complex, dual-hazard scenario requiring specialized procedures (e.g., air monitoring, retrieval systems) that a standard fall rescue plan would lack.
Incorrect: On-site teams can perform the rescue if properly trained and equipped.
Incorrect: ANSI Z359 provides guidelines for rescue, it does not prohibit vertical entry.
questions.explanation: This scenario highlights a failure in comprehensive hazard assessment, a key duty of the Competent Person. The rescue plan must be tailored to the specific situation. A fall rescue plan and a confined space rescue plan are not interchangeable. A worker suspended in a confined space may be exposed to toxic gases or an oxygen-deficient atmosphere, making the rescue far more complex and time-sensitive than a simple fall in open air.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference in purpose between a positioning system and a personal fall arrest system (PFAS)?
answers: Positioning systems use ropes, while PFAS use webbing.
A positioning system is designed to prevent a worker from reaching a fall hazard, while a PFAS arrests a fall that is already in progress.
Positioning systems only require a body belt, while PFAS requires a full-body harness.
A PFAS must limit arrest forces to 1,800 lbs, while a positioning system has no force limitations.
feedbacks: Incorrect: Both systems can use either ropes or webbing.

Correct: This is the core distinction. Positioning (also called restraint) keeps a worker in a safe area or supported, preventing any fall from occurring. Fall arrest activates only after a fall has begun.
Incorrect: While partially true (body belts can be used for positioning), the fundamental difference is function, not just components.
Incorrect: Positioning systems have their own strength requirements (e.g., 3,000 lbs anchorage) but are not designed for dynamic loading.
questions.explanation: This is a foundational concept for a Competent Person. A positioning system (per 1926.502(e)) supports a worker at a location, leaving their hands free, and is not designed to arrest a fall (e.g., rebar tying). A fall restraint system prevents the worker from reaching the fall hazard. A personal fall arrest system (PFAS) (per 1926.502(d)) does nothing until a fall occurs, at which point it is designed to safely stop the fall.

questions.question: A toeboard installed as part of a guardrail system must be a minimum of how high, and be able to withstand what force?
answers: 3.5 inches high; 50 pounds of force.
4 inches high; 100 pounds of force.
3 inches high; 25 pounds of force.
4.5 inches high; 50 pounds of force.
feedbacks: Correct: 1926.502(b)(13) and (j)(2) require toeboards to be a minimum of 3.5 inches in height and capable of withstanding a force of 50 pounds applied in any downward or outward direction.
Incorrect: The height and force requirements are lower than this.
Incorrect: The height and force requirements are higher than this.
Incorrect: The minimum height is 3.5 inches, not 4.5 inches.
questions.explanation: The specifications for toeboards are precise in Subpart M. The minimum 3.5-inch height (nominal lumber size of 2x4) is designed to prevent tools and materials from rolling off the edge. The 50-pound force requirement ensures it won't fail if struck by a sliding object or accidentally kicked. This is detailed in 1926.502(j).

questions.question: A competent person approves the use of a single, standard 6-foot shock-absorbing lanyard to be used as part of a horizontal lifeline between two stanchions. Why is this a critical error?
answers: The lanyard is too short to provide adequate mobility.
The lanyard's shock absorber is not designed for the increased fall forces of an HLL.
The snap hooks on the lanyard are not compatible with the stanchions.
The lanyard is not made of wire rope.
feedbacks: Incorrect: Mobility is not the life-safety issue here.

Correct: A fall on a flexible horizontal lifeline creates greater fall distances and higher arresting forces than a fall on a rigid anchor point. A standard lanyard's energy absorber may be insufficient or could fully deploy, transmitting excessive force to the worker.
Incorrect: While compatibility is important, the fundamental error is the misuse of the lanyard in this type of system.
Incorrect: Lanyards are typically made of webbing or synthetic rope, not wire rope.
questions.explanation: This is a common and deadly misconception. A horizontal lifeline (HLL) has sag, which increases both the fall distance and the forces generated during fall arrest. A standard personal energy absorber is calibrated for a fall on a rigid anchor. Using it on an HLL can lead to forces exceeding the 1,800 lb limit on the worker and can cause catastrophic system failure. Specialized HLL systems are required.

questions.question: Under what specific condition is it permissible to use a single 2x4 piece of lumber as a top rail for a guardrail system?
answers: When the posts are spaced no more than 6 feet apart.
When the '2-inch' dimension is oriented vertically, not horizontally.
When the wood is pressure-treated for outdoor use.
It is never permissible; two stacked 2x4s are always required.
feedbacks: Incorrect: Closer spacing helps, but is not the sole determining factor.

Correct: To utilize the full strength of the lumber, the 4-inch dimension should be vertical to resist downward force (like a floor joist). OSHA allows this if the wood is oriented to its stronger axis.
Incorrect: Treatment affects durability, not the structural strength needed to meet the 200 lb force test.
Incorrect: A single 2x4 can be compliant if it meets the performance test, which is much more likely when oriented correctly.
questions.explanation: OSHA's guardrail standard is performance-based. It must hold 200 lbs. While Appendix B to Subpart M provides examples (e.g., 2x4s), the key is meeting the performance requirement. A 2x4 laid flat is weak and will likely fail the 200 lb test. A 2x4 on its edge (with the 3.5" nominal dimension oriented vertically) is significantly stronger and more likely to meet the requirement, especially with appropriate post spacing. A competent person must understand this structural principle.

questions.question: A roofing contractor is using a safety monitoring system on a low-slope roof (4:12 pitch) with a width of 48 feet. According to 1926.502(h), what is the maximum number of workers a single safety monitor can be responsible for?
answers: 2 workers
4 workers
There is no specific limit, as long as the monitor can see them and is in communication.
The limit is one monitor per 50 feet of roof edge.
feedbacks: Incorrect: There is no limit of two workers.
Incorrect: There is no limit of four workers.

Correct: 1926.502(h)(1)(v) states the monitor shall be on the same level and within visual sighting distance and be able to communicate orally. It does not set a numerical limit, making it a judgment call for the competent person based on site conditions.
Incorrect: This is a misinterpretation of the rule that no worker shall be more than 50 feet from the monitor.
questions.explanation: The OSHA standard for safety monitors is performance-oriented. It requires the monitor to be able to see and hear the workers they are responsible for and to have no other distracting duties. It does not set a hard number (e.g., '6 workers'). The competent person must assess the specific site (roof size, obstructions, noise level) to determine how many workers one monitor can *effectively* and safely oversee at one time.

questions.question: During a harness inspection, the competent person finds that the fall arrest indicator, a patch of folded and stitched webbing, has been deployed. The worker claims he just 'snagged it on a nail' and didn't fall. What is the correct action?
answers: Ask the worker to sign a statement, then put the harness back in service.
Test the indicator by pulling on it to see if it deploys further.
Immediately remove the harness from service for disposal or recertification by the manufacturer.
Cut off the deployed indicator tag and continue to use the harness.
feedbacks: Incorrect: The physical evidence of the deployed indicator overrides the worker's statement.
Incorrect: This serves no purpose and could further damage the harness.

Correct: A deployed fall arrest indicator means the harness has been subjected to forces that require it to be removed from service, regardless of the cause. Its purpose is to provide a non-negotiable signal of impact.
Incorrect: This is a willful violation that deliberately circumvents a critical safety feature.
questions.explanation: Fall arrest indicators are designed as a simple, unambiguous way to identify if a harness has been subjected to an impact load. Per 1926.502(d)(21) and all manufacturer instructions, once this indicator is deployed—for any reason—the harness must be immediately removed from service. It is considered compromised until it can be recertified by the manufacturer or an authorized agent.

questions.question: A competent person is developing a rescue plan for workers on a 60-foot-high scaffold. The plan is to use a stocked rescue kit containing a remote-reach pole and a 4:1 pulley system. The kit has been sealed since it was purchased 2 years ago. Why is this plan potentially deficient?
answers: A 4:1 pulley system is insufficient for a 60-foot height.
Scaffold rescues must be performed by the fire department.
The equipment has never been unsealed, inspected, or practiced with by the designated rescuers.
The plan must include a self-rescue component using a trauma strap.
feedbacks: Incorrect: The mechanical advantage is independent of the height; the issue is rope length and user proficiency.
Incorrect: On-site teams are the preferred and often required method for prompt rescue.
Correct: Rescue equipment must be periodically inspected (even in storage) and, more importantly, the rescue team must have hands-on practice to be proficient and ensure a 'prompt rescue'.
Incorrect: While trauma straps are vital, they are for the victim to use while awaiting rescue, not a substitute for the rescue plan itself.
questions.explanation: A rescue plan is not just a document; it's a capability. A sealed kit represents an unknown. The equipment could have degraded, ropes could be tangled, or components could be missing. More critically, per ANSI Z359.2, rescue proficiency is a perishable skill. A team that has never practiced with their specific equipment cannot be expected to perform a high-stress rescue 'promptly' as required by 1926.502(d)(20).

questions.question: When are self-retracting lifelines (SRLs) required to be recertified by the manufacturer or an authorized repair center? (Select TWO)
answers: After any fall event or impact load, including a sharp, sudden lock-up.
At regular intervals specified by the manufacturer (e.g., annually or biennially).
Every time a new employee uses the device.
If the housing gets a cosmetic scratch that does not affect function.
After being used in a dusty environment, even if cleaned.
feedbacks: Correct: Per 1926.502(d)(21) and manufacturer requirements, any impact requires removal from service and professional inspection/recertification.
Correct: Most manufacturers mandate periodic recertification for complex mechanical devices like SRLs to ensure internal components are sound.
Incorrect: This is not required. User inspection before each use is the requirement.
Incorrect: Minor cosmetic damage is not a trigger for recertification, though it should be noted in inspection logs.
Incorrect: Environmental exposure requires more frequent user-level inspection but not automatic recertification unless damage is found.
questions.explanation: SRLs are complex mechanical devices with internal brakes, springs, and clutches. A competent person must understand there are two triggers for professional recertification: 1) Event-based: any time the unit is subjected to an impact load, and 2) Time-based: according to the manufacturer's required service schedule. Both are essential for ensuring the device will function correctly in a fall.

questions.question: A guardrail system is being installed around the perimeter of a 10th-floor balcony. Which of the following components is required by 1926 Subpart M in this specific situation that might not be required on a low-slope roof?
answers: A midrail.
A toeboard.
A top rail capable of withstanding 200 lbs of force.
Post spacing of no more than 8 feet.
feedbacks: Incorrect: A midrail is always a required component of a standard guardrail system.

Correct: Per 1926.501(b)(1), fall protection is required. To prevent tools/materials from falling onto people below, a toeboard is essential and required under 1926.502(j)(1) when there is a risk of falling objects.
Incorrect: This is always a required component of a standard guardrail system.
Incorrect: This is always a required component of a standard guardrail system.
questions.explanation: While guardrails always require a top rail and midrail, the requirement for a toeboard is conditional. 1926.502(j)(1) states that toeboards are required when 'there is a hazard of tools, materials, or equipment falling from a higher to a lower level.' A 10th-floor balcony over a public area presents a very high risk of this, making a toeboard mandatory. On an isolated roof with no one below, it might not be.

questions.question: A new type of 'smart harness' with integrated sensors is introduced on site. The Competent Person has been trained on traditional harnesses but not this new model. What is the CP's immediate responsibility before allowing its use?
answers: Assume it works like a normal harness and approve its use.
Prohibit its use until the manufacturer provides a discount.
Receive training from the manufacturer or a qualified representative on its specific inspection, use, limitations, and sensor functions.
Allow workers to use it but require them to read the instruction manual first.
feedbacks: Incorrect: A CP cannot assume competence with new technology.
Incorrect: Cost is not a safety consideration.

Correct: The definition of a Competent Person requires them to have knowledge to identify hazards. For new technology, this knowledge must be acquired through specific training before they can oversee its use.
Incorrect: Simply reading a manual is not a substitute for the CP's own competence and ability to train and supervise others.
questions.explanation: A Competent Person's authority stems from their knowledge and training. When novel equipment is introduced, their existing knowledge may be insufficient. It is their professional duty, as defined by 1926.32(f), to obtain the necessary training to understand the new device's functions, failure modes, inspection criteria, and limitations. They cannot effectively identify hazards or ensure proper use without this specific training.

questions.question: Which of the following anchorage points is explicitly PROHIBITED for use with a personal fall arrest system under Subpart M?
answers: A certified anchor point designed by a qualified person with a 2:1 safety factor.
An I-beam that a competent person has verified can support 5,000 lbs.
The top rail of a standard guardrail system.
A dedicated steel 'D-ring' anchor welded to a structural column.
feedbacks: Incorrect: This is the definition of a compliant, engineered anchor point per 1926.502(d)(15)(i).
Incorrect: This is the definition of a compliant, non-certified anchor point per 1926.502(d)(15)(ii).
Correct: 1926.502(d)(23) explicitly states that PFAS shall not be attached to guardrail systems, except under very specific circumstances for horizontal lifelines designed by a qualified person.
Incorrect: This is a common and acceptable type of engineered anchorage point.
questions.explanation: This is a critical, black-and-white rule. Guardrails are designed to withstand a 200-pound static load, not the dynamic impact of a fall arrest, which can be up to 1,800 lbs with an energy absorber. Attaching a PFAS to a guardrail could cause the entire guardrail section to fail, leading to a catastrophic accident. 1926.502(d)(23) makes this prohibition clear.

questions.question: A safety net is installed 12 feet below the working surface. According to the table in 1926.502(c)(2), what is the MINIMUM horizontal distance the outer edge of the net must extend from the edge of the working surface?
answers: 8 feet
10 feet
13 feet
15 feet
feedbacks: Incorrect: 8 feet is for falls up to 10 feet. This fall distance is greater.
Incorrect: 10 feet is the required extension for a fall of 'more than 10 feet up to 30 feet' per the 1994 standard. The current table has changed.
Correct: Per the table in 1926.502(c)(2), for a vertical distance of 'More than 10 feet', the minimum required horizontal distance is 13 feet.
Incorrect: This exceeds the minimum requirement.
questions.explanation: The Competent Person must be able to read and apply the table in 1926.502(c)(2) correctly. The table dictates the required horizontal projection of the net based on the vertical drop distance to account for a worker's trajectory. For a vertical drop of 12 feet (which is in the 'More than 10 feet' category), the table explicitly requires the net to extend 13 feet horizontally from the working edge.

questions.question: A worker using a body harness has a BMI of 42 and weighs 340 lbs. The PFAS system components (harness, lanyard, anchor) are all rated for a capacity up to 310 lbs. What is the critical compliance issue?
answers: The system is non-compliant because the user's weight exceeds the capacity of the components.
The system is compliant if the worker uses two lanyards.
The system is compliant if a qualified person approves it.
The system is compliant as long as the free fall distance is limited to 2 feet.
feedbacks: Correct: PFAS components are tested and rated for a specific capacity range (typically up to 310 lbs). Use by a heavier worker is outside the tested limits and invalidates the system's compliance.
Incorrect: Using two lanyards does not change the weight capacity of the individual components or how they are tested.
Incorrect: A qualified person cannot approve the use of equipment outside of its manufacturer-rated and tested capacity.
Incorrect: Limiting free fall is good practice but does not solve the fundamental problem of the equipment not being rated for the user's weight.
questions.explanation: OSHA and ANSI standards for PFAS are based on tests using a specific range of weights, with 310 lbs being a common upper limit for standard equipment. A worker weighing more than the rated capacity of *any* component in the system creates an unsafe condition. The fall arrest forces could exceed 1,800 lbs, and the equipment itself could fail. Specialized equipment rated for higher capacities is required. A competent person must verify this compatibility.

questions.question: During a leading-edge steel erection project, a worker is using a 6-foot energy-absorbing lanyard designed for a 6-foot free fall. The anchorage point is at foot level. What is the most critical and immediate violation a Competent Person must identify?
answers: The lanyard is too short for the task.
The anchorage point is not certified.
The free fall distance exceeds the lanyard's design limit.
The worker is not using an SRL.
feedbacks: Incorrect: The length is standard, but its application in this scenario is the primary issue.
Incorrect: Certification is a separate issue; the immediate danger is the free fall distance.
Correct: A foot-level anchor creates a free fall of nearly 6 feet, plus body height to D-ring, exceeding the lanyard's 6-foot limit and violating 1926.502(d)(16)(iii).
Incorrect: An SRL is an option, but the core violation is the excessive free fall created by the chosen system.
questions.explanation: With a foot-level anchorage, a worker falling over the edge will fall their lanyard length (6 ft) plus the distance from their feet to their back D-ring (~5 ft), resulting in an ~11-foot free fall. This exceeds the 6-foot free fall limit for standard lanyards, violating 1926.502(d)(16)(iii) and requiring a specific leading-edge rated device.

questions.question: A competent person is evaluating a non-certified anchorage point for a single personal fall arrest system (PFAS). The anchor is a steel I-beam. According to 1926.502(d)(15), what is the minimum standard this anchorage must meet without certification by a qualified person?
answers: It must support 3,600 lbs without failure.
It must be capable of supporting a load of 5,000 lbs.
It must support twice the maximum potential impact load.
It must be approved in writing by the site superintendent.
feedbacks: Incorrect: 3,600 lbs is the gate strength requirement for certain snap hooks, not the anchorage strength requirement under this provision.
Correct: 1926.502(d)(15)(ii) requires non-certified anchorages to be capable of supporting a static load of 5,000 pounds per employee attached.
Incorrect: This '2-to-1 safety factor' applies only to certified anchorages designed by a qualified person per 1926.502(d)(15)(i).
Incorrect: Site superintendent approval does not substitute for the strength requirements outlined in the OSHA standard.
questions.explanation: OSHA 1926.502(d)(15) provides two paths for anchorage points. If not designed by a qualified person (certified), the anchorage must have a strength capable of supporting a static load of 5,000 lbs per employee. The 2-to-1 safety factor is for engineered (certified) systems.

questions.question: A temporary guardrail system is constructed using 2x4 lumber. The top rail is 43 inches high, and the midrail is 21 inches high. The vertical posts are spaced 10 feet apart. Which of these factors makes the guardrail non-compliant with 1926 Subpart M?
answers: The top rail height.
The midrail height.
The material used (2x4 lumber).
The spacing of the vertical posts.
feedbacks: Incorrect: The top rail height of 43 inches falls within the acceptable range of 42 inches +/- 3 inches per 1926.502(b)(1).
Incorrect: The midrail height of 21 inches is approximately midway between the top rail and the walking surface, which is compliant per 1926.502(b)(2).
Incorrect: 2x4 lumber is a common and acceptable material, provided it meets the strength requirements.
Correct: 1926.502(b)(3) states that intermediate members (posts) must be spaced no more than 8 feet apart on centers.
questions.explanation: While the height and materials may be acceptable, the structural integrity of a guardrail is highly dependent on post spacing. Spacing posts at 10 feet apart, instead of the maximum 8 feet required by 1926.502(b)(3), would likely cause the rail to fail the 200-pound force test.

questions.question: A worker falls into a safety net installed 8 feet below the working surface. According to OSHA 1926.502(c), what is the minimum required horizontal distance the outer edge of the net must extend from the edge of the working surface?
answers: 5 feet
8 feet
10 feet
13 feet
feedbacks: Incorrect: This is insufficient for a drop distance of 8 feet.
Correct: For falls up to 10 feet, the net must extend 8 feet horizontally from the edge of the working surface per the table in 1926.502(c)(2).
Incorrect: 10 feet of horizontal extension is required for drops greater than 10 feet.
Incorrect: 13 feet of horizontal extension is required for drops greater than 10 feet.
questions.explanation: OSHA standard 1926.502(c)(2) provides a table that dictates the required horizontal extension of a safety net based on the vertical distance from the working level to the net. For a vertical distance of 'over 5 feet up to 10 feet', the minimum required horizontal distance is 8 feet.

questions.question: A competent person observes an employee using a body belt for fall arrest on a scaffold 15 feet high. Which TWO of the following statements are true regarding this situation?
answers: This is compliant if the worker weighs less than 180 lbs.
The competent person must immediately stop the work.
This is compliant if a qualified person approved the system.
The use of a body belt for fall arrest is explicitly prohibited.
The system is compliant if used with a shock-absorbing lanyard.
feedbacks: Incorrect: Body belts have been prohibited for use in fall arrest systems since January 1, 1998, regardless of worker weight.
Correct: This is a life-threatening violation, and the competent person has the authority and responsibility to halt work immediately per 1926.32(f).
Incorrect: A qualified person cannot approve a system that is explicitly prohibited by an OSHA standard.
Correct: 1926.502(d) states that body belts are not acceptable as part of a personal fall arrest system. They may only be used for positioning.
Incorrect: A shock-absorbing lanyard does not make a prohibited component (the body belt) acceptable for fall arrest.
questions.explanation: The use of body belts for fall arrest has been strictly prohibited since 1998 due to the high risk of internal injuries upon fall impact. 1926.502(d) explicitly forbids their use in PFAS. A competent person's primary duty under 1926.32(f) is to identify such hazards and take immediate corrective action, including stopping the work.

questions.question: During the semi-annual competent person inspection of fall protection equipment, which THREE of the following discoveries would require a harness to be immediately removed from service?
answers: A faded manufacturer's tag where the date is illegible.
Minor discoloration from sunlight on the shoulder straps.
A 1/8 inch deep cut on the edge of the webbing.
A D-ring with light surface rust that can be wiped off.
Pitting and corrosion on a friction buckle that impedes adjustment.
feedbacks: Correct: An illegible tag prevents verification of the harness's age and inspection history, requiring its removal per ANSI standards and manufacturer instructions.
Incorrect: UV discoloration is a sign of degradation, but minor fading alone is not typically a removal criterion unless the webbing feels brittle.
Correct: Any cut, fraying, or abrasion that penetrates the outer surface of the webbing compromises its strength and requires removal from service per 1926.502(d)(21).
Incorrect: Light surface rust that does not cause pitting or interfere with function is generally acceptable, though it should be cleaned and monitored.
Correct: Corrosion that causes pitting or interferes with the mechanical function of any hardware is a critical defect requiring immediate removal.
questions.explanation: Equipment must be removed from service if any component is defective. This includes damaged webbing (cuts, frays, burns), compromised hardware (corrosion, pits, cracks, deformation), and illegible or missing labels that prevent critical tracking and verification, as outlined in 1926.502(d)(21) and ANSI Z359.

questions.question: A rescue plan for a worker suspended in a PFAS must ensure rescue occurs 'promptly'. While OSHA does not define 'promptly' in minutes, what is the primary medical concern that this requirement aims to prevent?
answers: Dehydration
Hypothermia
Spinal cord injury from the fall impact.
Suspension Trauma (Orthostatic Intolerance)
feedbacks: Incorrect: While a concern in prolonged events, it is not the immediate, life-threatening condition addressed by 'prompt' rescue.
Incorrect: Hypothermia is a risk but is secondary to the immediate circulatory issue.
Incorrect: This injury would have occurred on impact; the rescue timing is to prevent post-fall complications.
Correct: This is a life-threatening condition where blood pools in the legs, starving the brain and vital organs of oxygen, and can occur within minutes.
questions.explanation: The requirement for 'prompt rescue' in 1926.502(d)(20) is primarily to prevent suspension trauma, also known as orthostatic intolerance. This medical emergency occurs when a suspended person is immobile, leading to blood pooling in the lower extremities, which can cause unconsciousness and death in a very short time frame.

questions.question: When a qualified person designs an engineered horizontal lifeline (HLL) system, they must factor in the number of users and the initial sag. What is a critical consequence of excessive initial sag (catenary) in an HLL?
answers: It increases the required anchorage strength exponentially.
It reduces the free fall distance for the worker.
It makes the system cheaper to install.
It violates the 1926 Subpart L scaffold regulations.
feedbacks: Correct: Greater sag increases the horizontal forces exerted on the anchor points during a fall, often requiring significantly stronger anchorages.
Incorrect: Excessive sag actually increases the total fall distance, as the line itself will drop further during a fall.
Incorrect: While it may seem so, the increased load on anchorages can make the overall system more expensive and complex to design safely.
Incorrect: This is a Subpart M issue related to fall arrest systems, not a scaffold-specific regulation.
questions.explanation: In an HLL, the angle of the lifeline from the horizontal plane is critical. Excessive sag creates a very small angle, and the physics of force resolution dictate that as this angle decreases, the horizontal force vector on the anchorages increases exponentially. This is a key calculation for a qualified person per ANSI Z359.6.

questions.question: A wire rope guardrail's top rope is sagging 4 inches mid-span when a 150 lb force is applied. The posts are 8 feet apart. Is this compliant?
answers: Yes, as long as it returns to 42 inches when the force is removed.
No, the maximum allowable deflection is 3 inches.
Yes, because the force applied is less than the 200 lb test force.
No, the top rail must not deflect to a height less than 39 inches.
feedbacks: Incorrect: The deflection under load is the key test, not its return position.
Incorrect: The deflection limit is related to the top rail height, not a fixed value of 3 inches.
Incorrect: The test must prove it can withstand 200 lbs without excessive deflection. This partial test is inconclusive.

Correct: Per 1926.502(b)(4), the top rail must remain at a height of at least 39 inches under a 200 lb load. A 4-inch sag from a 42-inch starting height would bring it to 38 inches, which is a failure.
questions.explanation: The performance requirement for a guardrail top rail is two-fold: it must withstand a 200-pound force and not deflect to a height below 39 inches above the walking/working level. If the rail starts at 42 inches, a 4-inch deflection brings it to 38 inches, which is non-compliant with 1926.502(b)(4). The fact that this happened with only 150 lbs suggests it would fail catastrophically under the full 200 lb test.

questions.question: A safety net is being installed to protect workers on a bridge project. The net has a 5,000 lb minimum breaking strength, and the mesh openings are 6 inches by 6 inches. The Competent Person is conducting a drop test. What is the MINIMUM weight and drop height for this test?
answers: 200-pound bag of sand dropped from 25 feet.
400-pound bag of sand dropped from the working level, but no less than 42 inches.
500-pound steel weight dropped from 10 feet.
A drop test is only required if the net is not certified by the manufacturer.
feedbacks: Incorrect: The weight is too low for the standard drop test.
Correct: 1926.502(c)(4)(i) specifies a drop test with a 400-pound bag of sand, approximately 30 inches in diameter, dropped from the working level or 42 inches above, whichever is greater.
Incorrect: The standard specifies a bag of sand to simulate a body, not a concentrated steel weight.
Incorrect: A drop test is required after initial installation, after any repairs, and after relocation, regardless of manufacturer certification.
questions.explanation: OSHA 1926.502(c)(4)(i) is very specific about the drop test procedure to certify a safety net installation. It mandates a 400-pound bag of sand (28-32 inches in diameter) dropped from the same height as the walking/working surface, but not from less than 42 inches above that level, to ensure the net and its anchorages can absorb the impact.

questions.question: A competent person is creating a fall protection plan for a precast concrete erection project where conventional fall protection is infeasible. Which of the following elements are MANDATORY to include in this written, site-specific plan? (Select THREE)
answers: Identification of a designated 'Controlled Access Zone' (CAZ).
The signature of a registered Professional Engineer.
A detailed rescue plan to be implemented in the event of a fall.
A statement of why conventional fall protection is infeasible.
The names of every employee authorized to work in the area.
A copy of the company's general safety manual.
feedbacks: Correct: For leading edge and precast work, defining a CAZ is a core component of the plan per 1926.502(k)(7).
Incorrect: A 'qualified person' must develop the plan; this person is not required to be a P.E. unless the plan involves engineering new anchorages.
Correct: A rescue plan is a mandatory part of any fall protection program, especially one under a specialized plan, per 1926.502(k)(6).
Correct: The plan must explicitly document the reasons why systems like guardrails, nets, or PFAS cannot be used, as required by 1926.502(k)(1).
Incorrect: While the plan must identify who is authorized, listing every single name is not a specific requirement; this is usually handled via daily briefings or rosters.
Incorrect: The plan must be site-specific; a general manual is not sufficient.
questions.explanation: According to 1926.502(k), a fall protection plan is a last resort and must be highly detailed. It requires, at a minimum, documentation of infeasibility, the implementation of a controlled access zone (CAZ), and a clear rescue plan. These elements ensure that even without conventional systems, risks are controlled and emergency response is planned.

questions.question: A worker's full-body harness was stored in a job box with a leaking can of hydraulic fluid. The webbing is heavily stained but not cut or frayed. What is the correct action?
answers: Clean the harness with soap and water and return to service.
Note the stain in the inspection log and continue to use the harness.
Immediately remove the harness from service permanently.
Send the harness to a third-party lab for strength testing.
feedbacks: Incorrect: Soap and water may not remove the fluid, which can degrade the synthetic fibers over time.
Incorrect: The potential for chemical damage cannot be ignored; this is a reason for removal, not just documentation.

Correct: Chemical contamination (especially from petroleum distillates or corrosives) can weaken the webbing's synthetic fibers in ways that are not visible. Per 1926.502(d)(21), it must be removed from service.
Incorrect: This is not a practical or required step. The precautionary principle dictates removal from service.
questions.explanation: OSHA 1926.502(d)(21) requires that any fall arrest system subjected to impact loading be immediately removed from service. By extension, any condition that could compromise its integrity, such as chemical contamination, also requires removal. Manufacturers universally warn that solvents and hydraulic fluids can cause unseen damage to nylon/polyester webbing.

questions.question: The on-site rescue plan for a crew working 150 feet high on a communication tower states that in the event of a fall, the crew will call 911 and wait for the local fire department. The nearest fire station with high-angle rescue capabilities is 25 minutes away. Why is this plan non-compliant?
answers: The plan was not signed by a qualified person.
The plan relies solely on an off-site rescue service without ensuring their availability and capability.
The plan does not include provisions for self-rescue.
Employees were not trained on this specific plan.
feedbacks: Incorrect: Signature is a documentation issue; the primary flaw is the plan's content and feasibility.
Correct: 1926.502(d)(20) requires 'prompt rescue.' Relying on a distant 911 service without prior coordination and verification that they can perform the rescue in a timely manner is a violation.
Incorrect: While self-rescue is ideal, it's not always possible and its absence doesn't invalidate the entire plan if assisted rescue is adequate.
Incorrect: This is a training violation, but the plan itself is flawed at its core due to the time delay.
questions.explanation: 1926.502(d)(20) requires the employer to provide for 'prompt rescue.' The non-mandatory Appendix C clarifies that relying on 911 is not acceptable unless the employer has verified that the emergency service is available, capable, and willing to perform the specific type of rescue required in the necessary timeframe. A 25-minute response time is not 'prompt' and exposes the fallen worker to severe suspension trauma.

questions.question: A horizontal lifeline is installed between two non-certified I-beam anchorages 40 feet apart. A competent person is evaluating the system for one user. What TWO factors are most critical for the competent person to verify HAVE BEEN addressed by a qualified person?
answers: The D-ring on the user's harness is made of forged alloy steel.
The lifeline has been flagged every 6 feet for visibility.
The maximum arresting force (MAF) imposed on the user.
The calculated horizontal force that will be applied to the anchorages during a fall.
The calculated total fall distance, including lifeline sag.
The lifeline is a minimum of 1/2-inch diameter wire rope.
feedbacks: Incorrect: This is a standard harness feature and not part of the HLL design calculation.
Incorrect: While good practice, this is a wire rope guardrail requirement, not a primary HLL engineering concern.
Incorrect: The MAF is limited by the PFAS (e.g., 1,800 lbs), not determined by the HLL design itself, although the HLL design must account for it.
Correct: This is the most critical calculation, as horizontal forces can be many times the arresting force and are not intuitive. This requires a qualified person.
Correct: The dynamic sag of the HLL during a fall significantly increases the total fall distance and must be calculated to ensure the worker does not impact a lower level.
Incorrect: The required diameter depends on the specific engineering calculations, not a single minimum size.
questions.explanation: Designing a horizontal lifeline system is outside the scope of a competent person and must be done by a qualified person. The CP's role is to ensure that design has occurred. The two most critical outputs of that design are the massive horizontal forces generated at the anchors (which often require structural upgrades) and the total fall clearance needed, which includes the significant dynamic sag of the HLL during a fall. Miscalculating either can be catastrophic.

questions.question: A guardrail system on a flat roof is being used as the primary fall protection. What is the minimum distance it must be placed from the edge of the roof to also eliminate the need for a warning line system for roofing work?
answers: 2 feet
6 feet
10 feet
There is no distance; if a guardrail is present at the edge, no warning line is needed.
feedbacks: Incorrect: This distance is insufficient to remove the warning line requirement.
Incorrect: This is the distance from the edge where a warning line is typically placed for roofers working towards it.
Incorrect: This is the distance from the edge where a safety monitor can be used when moving away from the edge.
Correct: A compliant guardrail system installed at the edge of the roof is a form of conventional fall protection. It completely replaces the need for a warning line system under 1926.501(b)(10).
questions.explanation: A warning line system, as described in 1926.502(f), is an alternative for low-slope roofing work when conventional systems like guardrails are not used at the edge. If a fully compliant guardrail system is installed at the edge, it serves as the primary fall protection, and the entire area inside the guardrail is considered protected. Therefore, a warning line is not required.

questions.question: During a safety net drop test, the 400-lb sandbag is dropped from the working level 45 feet above the net. The bag deflects the net and momentarily touches a cross-beam located 12 feet below the net. What is the status of this installation?
answers: The test is a pass, as the net did not break.
The test is invalid and must be repeated with a 500-lb bag.
The installation has failed and must be re-rigged to provide greater clearance.
The test is a pass, but the cross-beam must be padded.
feedbacks: Incorrect: The primary purpose is to prevent contact with surfaces below, not just to avoid net failure.
Incorrect: The test parameters (400 lbs) were correct; the results indicated a failure.
Correct: 1926.502(c)(3) requires sufficient clearance under the net to prevent contact with any surface or structure below when impacted.
Incorrect: Padding a hazard does not meet the requirement to prevent contact with it.
questions.explanation: The clearance underneath a safety net is as critical as the net itself. The standard 1926.502(c)(3) explicitly requires that there be sufficient clearance to prevent a falling body from striking a lower level or obstruction. Contact with the cross-beam constitutes a test failure, and the net must be raised or the hazard removed before it can be certified for use.

questions.question: A competent person is authorized to make changes to the fall protection plan on site. When is the competent person REQUIRED to get a qualified person involved?
answers: When substituting one manufacturer's certified anchorage strap for another's.
When employees report feeling unsafe with the current system.
When a non-certified anchorage point needs to be used that is not a structural steel member.
When retraining is needed for a new employee.
feedbacks: Incorrect: This is a simple equipment substitution that a competent person can manage.
Incorrect: The CP should investigate, but this doesn't automatically require a QP unless a design flaw is identified.
Correct: Evaluating the capacity of non-obvious structures (e.g., concrete walls, equipment frames) requires engineering analysis and is the duty of a qualified person.
Incorrect: This is a core duty of a competent person.
questions.explanation: A competent person's authority is based on knowledge and experience to identify hazards and select/implement existing solutions. A qualified person has a degree, certificate, or professional standing and has demonstrated the ability to solve or design complex systems. Designing or certifying an ad-hoc anchorage point requires engineering calculations to determine its capacity, which falls squarely under the duties of a qualified person per 1926.32(m).

questions.question: An SRL has been subjected to a minor fall event where a worker slipped on a sloped roof but did not fall over the edge. The SRL locked up abruptly but did not deploy its energy absorber. What is the required action by the competent person?
answers: Since the energy absorber did not deploy, document the event and return it to service.
Spray the retraction mechanism with lubricant and test it three times.
Immediately remove the SRL from service and follow the manufacturer's instructions for inspection or disposal.
Tag the SRL 'For light-duty use only' and restrict its use to workers under 200 lbs.
feedbacks: Incorrect: Any event that causes an abrupt, high-speed lock-up is considered an impact load.
Incorrect: Field lubrication is generally prohibited by manufacturers.
Correct: Per 1926.502(d)(21) and all manufacturer requirements, any PFAS component subjected to impact loading (which includes a high-speed lock-up) must be removed from service immediately.
Incorrect: There is no such category as 'light-duty use' for damaged equipment. It is either serviceable or it is not.
questions.explanation: The standard 1926.502(d)(21) is absolute: any personal fall arrest system component subjected to impact loading shall be immediately removed from service. A sudden, sharp lock-up of an SRL, even if it doesn't involve a full fall over an edge, constitutes an impact load. The internal brake mechanism could be damaged, and it must be taken out of service until it is recertified by the a manufacturer or an authorized repair center.

questions.question: A rescue plan involves using a pre-rigged 3:1 mechanical advantage pulley system to lift a fallen worker. The competent person notes that the designated rescuers have been trained on the system but have not practiced with it in over a year. Why is this a potential failure point in the rescue plan?
answers: The pulley system should be a 5:1 ratio for a single rescuer.
The plan is non-compliant because it does not involve calling 911 as a backup.
Rescue proficiency is perishable, and lack of practice can lead to critical delays or errors during an actual event.
Mechanical advantage systems are not permitted for human suspension.
feedbacks: Incorrect: The mechanical advantage ratio is part of the design; the issue here is human factors, not the specific ratio.
Incorrect: A capable on-site team can be the primary plan; 911 is not a mandatory backup.

Correct: OSHA's requirement for a functional rescue plan implies that rescuers must be proficient. Annual practice is a minimum industry best practice (e.g., ANSI Z359.2) to ensure the team can perform the rescue 'promptly' and effectively.
Incorrect: Such systems are standard for technical rescue, provided they use appropriate life-safety equipment.
questions.explanation: While 1926.502(d)(20) requires a plan for prompt rescue, the implicit requirement is that the plan is *viable*. Viability depends on both equipment and personnel proficiency. Rescue skills are perishable. A team that has not practiced in over a year cannot be reasonably expected to perform a complex, high-stress rescue 'promptly' or without error. Industry best practice, reflected in ANSI Z359.2, calls for regular, hands-on practice.

questions.question: When calculating total fall distance for a worker using a 6-foot energy-absorbing lanyard, which THREE of the following components must be included in the calculation?
answers: The length of the lanyard (6 feet).
The deceleration distance (max 3.5 feet).
The worker's weight.
The height of the anchorage point above the walking surface.
Harness stretch and D-ring shift (approx. 1 foot).
The cost of the fall arrest system.
feedbacks: Correct: This is the primary component of the free fall distance.
Correct: This is the distance the energy absorber deploys to arrest the fall.
Incorrect: The worker's weight affects the force, but not the distance components of this specific calculation (though it must be within the lanyard's limits).
Incorrect: The height of the anchorage determines the starting point, but it's not a component *added* to the fall distance itself.
Correct: The harness and body dynamics will add a small amount of distance during the arrest.
Incorrect: Cost is irrelevant to the physics of a fall.
questions.explanation: Calculating total fall distance is critical to ensure a worker will not impact a lower level. According to OSHA's non-mandatory Appendix C to Subpart M, the calculation must include: Lanyard Length + Deceleration Distance + Harness Stretch/D-Ring Shift + a Safety Factor. The first three are direct components of the fall itself. A Competent Person must account for all these to comply with 1926.502(d)(16).

questions.question: A guardrail is placed around an excavation that is 8 feet deep. The top rail is made of 3/8-inch wire rope, flagged every 6 feet. The top rope is tensioned to be 42 inches high. Why is this system potentially non-compliant?
answers: Excavations require solid barricades, not wire rope.
The wire rope must be at least 1/2-inch in diameter.
The wire rope is not flagged every 4 feet.
The system lacks a midrail and toeboard.
feedbacks: Incorrect: Guardrails are an acceptable barrier for excavations per Subpart P, which references Subpart M for specs.
Incorrect: 1926.502(b)(9) requires wire rope to be at least 1/4-inch diameter. 3/8-inch is compliant.
Incorrect: The requirement is flagging at intervals not to exceed 6 feet.
Correct: Per 1926.502(b), a guardrail system must have a top rail, midrail, and (if material can fall) a toeboard. A single top rope is not a complete guardrail system.
questions.explanation: A guardrail system, by definition in 1926.502(b), consists of a top rail, midrail, and vertical uprights. If there is a hazard of materials falling, it must also have a toeboard. A single wire rope, even if it meets the height and strength requirements for a top rail, is not a complete system and fails to protect against someone sliding under the rail, a violation of 1926.502(b)(2).

questions.question: According to the ANSI Z359.17-2023 standard, which is considered an industry best practice for leading-edge (LE) SRLs, what is a critical design feature that distinguishes them from standard SRLs?
answers: They have a minimum housing strength of 5,000 lbs.
They incorporate an energy absorber at the harness connection point.
They have an integrated trauma strap pack.
They are designed to withstand contact with a standardized sharp edge (e.g., 0.005" radius steel) without severing.
feedbacks: Incorrect: Housing strength is important but not the key distinguishing feature for LE use.
Incorrect: Most SRLs have an internal or external energy absorber; this is not unique to LE models.
Incorrect: Trauma straps are a separate harness feature, not an SRL feature.
Correct: The primary purpose and design test for an LE-rated SRL is its ability to resist being cut when a lifeline is dragged over a sharp edge during a fall.
questions.explanation: While not yet codified by OSHA, the ANSI Z359.14 standard for SRLs specifies rigorous testing for Leading-Edge (LE) models. The most critical test involves dropping a weight over a standardized steel bar with a radius of just 0.005 inches to simulate a worst-case scenario on steel decking. Standard SRLs would likely sever in this test, making this resistance the key distinguishing safety feature of an LE-SRL.

questions.question: A competent person is inspecting a permanently installed horizontal lifeline on a rooftop. The system was designed by a qualified person 5 years ago. What is the competent person's primary responsibility during this inspection?
answers: Re-calculate all the engineering loads to ensure they are still valid.
Visually inspect the system for defects and verify that the annual inspection by a qualified person is current.
Stress-test the system by attaching a 1,000 lb weight.
Rewrite the rescue plan to incorporate new technology.
feedbacks: Incorrect: Re-engineering the system is the duty of a qualified person, not a competent person.
Correct: The CP's role is to perform regular visual inspections for damage/defects and to ensure the system's required annual certification by a QP is up-to-date per ANSI Z359.6.
Incorrect: Field load testing is highly specialized and generally not performed unless specified by the engineer; it can damage the system.
Incorrect: While a good idea, the primary responsibility is to inspect the existing system's physical integrity and compliance status.
questions.explanation: For engineered systems like permanent HLLs, there is a two-tiered inspection process. The competent person performs frequent visual inspections (e.g., before each use). However, ANSI Z359.6, the standard for specifications and design requirements for active fall protection systems, mandates a formal recertification inspection at least annually by a qualified person. The CP must verify this recertification has been completed and documented, in addition to their own visual inspection for obvious damage.

questions.question: Which of these scenarios definitively REQUIRES a fall protection plan prepared by a qualified person because conventional systems are considered infeasible?
answers: Working on a 3:12 slope roof at a height of 20 feet.
Washing windows on the 3rd floor of a building using a boatswain's chair.
Erecting the final steel beam to complete a skeletal structure ('topping out').
Performing maintenance on an HVAC unit 15 feet from the edge of a 100-foot-wide flat roof.
feedbacks: Incorrect: This is a low-slope roof where conventional systems like guardrails, nets, or PFAS are typically feasible.
Incorrect: This work is covered under scaffold rules or requires a standard PFAS; it is not considered infeasible.
Correct: During certain steel erection activities, like connecting beams at the final point, the structure may not allow for conventional fall protection, requiring a plan under 1926.760(a)(2).
Incorrect: This situation can be managed with a warning line and safety monitor system.
questions.explanation: OSHA provides specific exceptions for when a fall protection plan can be used in lieu of conventional systems. One of the most common and explicit examples is during certain steel erection activities (1926 Subpart R) and precast concrete erection (1926.501(b)(12)), where installing guardrails or anchor points is demonstrably infeasible for a specific, short-term task. This requires a site-specific plan.

questions.question: A worker using a PFAS falls and is successfully arrested. They are suspended, conscious, and uninjured. They deploy their harness's trauma relief straps. What is the primary physiological function of these straps?
answers: They act as a tourniquet to stop potential bleeding.
They allow the worker to use their leg muscles to pump blood, counteracting venous pooling.
They convert the harness into a seat, making the wait more comfortable.
They send an electronic alert to the rescue team.
feedbacks: Incorrect: They are designed to relieve pressure, not apply it like a tourniquet.
Correct: By creating a loop to stand in, the worker can flex their leg muscles, which helps circulate the pooled blood in the legs and delays the onset of suspension trauma.
Incorrect: While they may increase comfort, their primary function is medical, not comfort. They do not function as a proper seat.
Incorrect: They are simple mechanical straps and have no electronic function.
questions.explanation: Trauma relief straps are a critical life-safety device for post-fall suspension. Their purpose is to fight suspension trauma (orthostatic intolerance). When a worker stands in the loops, they engage their leg muscles (the 'second heart'), which contract and squeeze the veins, forcing the pooled blood back toward the heart and brain, thus delaying loss of consciousness and allowing more time for rescue.

questions.question: On a multi-employer worksite, a Competent Person for the general contractor observes a plumbing subcontractor's employee using a PFAS with a frayed lanyard. What are the Competent Person's primary obligations? (Select TWO)
answers: Confiscate the subcontractor's equipment immediately.
Stop the affected employee's work and notify their supervisor of the hazard.
File a formal report with OSHA within 24 hours.
Assume no responsibility as the worker is not their direct employee.
Inform their own management and document the corrective action taken.
feedbacks: Incorrect: The CP does not have authority to confiscate another company's property, but they must prevent its use on site.
Correct: The controlling employer's CP has the authority and responsibility to stop any unsafe work and must inform the creating employer (the sub).
Incorrect: Reporting is for fatalities/severe injuries, not for hazard observation. The duty is to correct the hazard on site.
Incorrect: On a multi-employer worksite, the controlling contractor has a duty to ensure safety for all workers.
Correct: The CP must document the hazard and the steps taken to correct it, which includes notifying their own management chain.
questions.explanation: Under OSHA's Multi-Employer Worksite Policy, the controlling contractor's Competent Person has the authority and obligation to correct hazards created by other employers. The correct procedure is to stop the unsafe act and communicate the issue to both the subcontractor's supervision (the creating employer) and their own management (the controlling employer), while documenting the event.

questions.question: A worker is using an SRL anchored at foot level for leading-edge work. The clearance below the working surface is 16 feet to the ground. The SRL is a leading-edge model (SRL-LE). Why might this scenario still be non-compliant?
answers: The SRL is not designed for horizontal use.
The total fall distance may exceed the available clearance.
The worker weighs more than 310 lbs.
The anchorage point has not been certified by an engineer.
feedbacks: Incorrect: An SRL-LE is specifically designed for horizontal and leading-edge applications.
Correct: An SRL-LE has a longer deceleration distance than a standard SRL and, combined with free fall from a foot-level anchor, may require more than 16 feet of clearance.
Incorrect: While a valid concern, the critical issue in this specific scenario is the calculation of clearance distance.
Incorrect: Anchorage certification is a separate issue from the clearance calculation, which is the immediate life-threatening problem.
questions.explanation: Even with a leading-edge rated SRL (SRL-LE), the total fall distance calculation is critical. It includes freefall (approx. 5-6 ft from a foot-level anchor), the extended deceleration distance of the SRL-LE, harness stretch, and a safety factor. These combined can easily exceed 16 feet, meaning the worker would impact the ground. This violates 1926.502(d)(16).

questions.question: If a guardrail system is installed on a work platform and is subjected to high winds and used for equipment storage, what additional design consideration must a qualified person address beyond the standard 200 lb force requirement?
answers: The color of the guardrail must be high-visibility yellow.
The guardrail must meet both the 200 lb concentrated load and any anticipated wind/material loads.
The toeboard must be made of steel instead of wood.
The midrail must be replaced with steel mesh.
feedbacks: Incorrect: Color is a best practice for visibility but not a structural design requirement in this context.

Correct: 1926.502(b)(3) notes guardrails must withstand the 200 lb force, but general duty clause and engineering principles require they also be designed for any other loads they are expected to bear.
Incorrect: The material must be sufficient for the load, but steel is not explicitly required over wood.
Incorrect: Mesh is an option but not a requirement; the standard midrail is sufficient if no additional loads are applied to it.
questions.explanation: While 1926.502(b)(3) sets the minimum 200 lb point load, it assumes standard conditions. When additional, foreseeable loads like high winds or stacked materials are introduced, a qualified person must perform calculations to ensure the entire system (rails, posts, and fasteners) can withstand the combined forces without failure, per sound engineering practice and the General Duty Clause.

questions.question: When two safety nets are joined together, what is the OSHA requirement for the connection?
answers: They must overlap by a minimum of 24 inches.
They must be sewn together by a certified net repair facility.
They must be lashed or spliced together so the mesh spacing is not exceeded and there are no gaps.
They must be connected with a minimum of 20 zip ties per linear foot.
feedbacks: Incorrect: OSHA does not specify a minimum overlap distance.
Incorrect: While professional repair is an option, it's not the only method for joining nets on site.
Correct: 1926.502(c)(1) requires that connections between net panels are as strong as the integral net components and that the mesh spacing is maintained.
Incorrect: Zip ties are not an approved method for lashing load-bearing safety nets.
questions.explanation: The performance-based requirement in 1926.502(c)(1) focuses on the result, not the method. The goal is to create a continuous, single net system. The lashing or splicing must ensure that the junction is as strong as the rest of the net and that the mesh size does not increase, preventing a worker from falling through the connection point.

questions.question: A full-body harness has been in storage, unused, in a dry, dark container for 6 years. It is in visually perfect condition. The manufacturer's label is silent on a maximum service life. What is the correct action for the Competent Person?
answers: Return it to service, as there is no visible damage.
Destroy the harness immediately, as most manufacturers recommend a 5-year life.
Contact the manufacturer to determine their official policy on maximum service life for that model.
Tag it for 'light-duty use only' for workers under 180 lbs.
feedbacks: Incorrect: The absence of visible damage does not guarantee the integrity of aged synthetic fibers.
Incorrect: While 5-10 years is a common recommendation, it is not an OSHA rule, and the CP's action should be based on policy and verification.
Correct: The CP's duty is to follow manufacturer instructions. If they are missing or unclear, the CP must seek clarification from the source to make an informed decision.
Incorrect: There is no such classification for fall protection equipment; it is either serviceable or not.
questions.explanation: A Competent Person's responsibility under 1926.502(d)(21) and industry best practice (ANSI Z359) is to adhere to the manufacturer's instructions for the equipment. When a critical piece of information like service life is unknown, the CP cannot make an assumption. The only correct course of action is to obtain the official guidance from the manufacturer before allowing the equipment to be used.

questions.question: During a post-fall rescue, the rescue team plans to attach their system directly to the anchor point of the victim's PFAS. The victim weighs 220 lbs. What is the minimum capacity the anchor point must now have to support both the victim and the rescue operation?
answers: 5,000 lbs, because that is the standard for a PFAS anchor.
5,000 lbs, plus the weight of the rescuer.
Sufficient capacity to support the rescue loads, as determined by a qualified person.
The anchor cannot be reused and a new anchor must be established.
feedbacks: Incorrect: The original 5,000 lb requirement was for one user (the victim). The rescue operation adds new loads.
Incorrect: This simple addition does not account for the dynamic forces of the rescue operation or required safety factors.

Correct: Rescue systems introduce complex loads. The anchor's capacity must be re-evaluated by a qualified person to ensure it can handle the victim, rescuer(s), and any dynamic forces from the rescue itself, often requiring a safety factor of 5:1 or more.
Incorrect: The anchor can be used if a qualified person verifies it has sufficient capacity for the new, higher loads of the rescue operation.
questions.explanation: A rescue operation is a separate event from the initial fall arrest. It imposes different, often higher loads on the anchorage. A qualified person must assess the anchor to ensure it can support the combined static and dynamic loads of the victim and the rescue system (which may include rescuers, ropes, and mechanical advantage). This falls outside the prescriptive 5,000 lb rule for a single PFAS. This is a critical rescue planning element under 1926.502(d)(20).

questions.question: A worker is using a 30-foot self-retracting lifeline (SRL) anchored directly overhead. They walk 20 feet horizontally away from the anchor point to perform a task near an edge. What is the primary fall hazard created by this situation?
answers: Excessive free fall distance.
The SRL lifeline is not rated for horizontal use.
A significant pendulum swing (swing fall) hazard.
Exceeding the SRL's maximum deployment length.
feedbacks: Incorrect: Since the anchor is overhead, the free fall distance will be minimal as the SRL should lock quickly.
Incorrect: The hazard exists even with a horizontally-rated SRL; the issue is the geometry of the fall.
Correct: A fall from this position would cause the worker to swing back toward the anchor point like a pendulum, potentially striking the structure with high force.
Incorrect: The worker is only 20 feet away, well within the 30-foot capacity of the SRL.
questions.explanation: Swing fall is a critical and often misunderstood hazard. While the vertical fall distance may be small, the horizontal distance from the anchor creates a large pendulum arc. The force of striking a column, wall, or other structure during the swing can be as deadly as the fall itself. A competent person must recognize this and ensure anchors are positioned as close to directly overhead as possible, per 1926.502(d)(17).

questions.question: A guardrail system on a ramp with a 15-degree slope must have its top rail height measured how?
answers: Vertically from the ramp surface to the rail, maintaining 42 inches +/- 3 inches along the entire length.
42 inches at the posts and allowed to sag in between.
Perpendicular to the ramp surface, which would be slightly less than a true vertical 42 inches.
42 inches at the top of the ramp and 42 inches at the bottom, with a straight line between.
feedbacks: Correct: 1926.502(b)(1) requires the height to be measured vertically from the walking/working surface. On a slope, this means the rail must be parallel to the ramp surface.
Incorrect: The height must be maintained along the entire length, not just at the posts.
Incorrect: Measurements must be true vertical to ensure proper protection height.
Incorrect: This would result in a non-parallel rail that is too low in the middle of the ramp.
questions.explanation: The principle of 1926.502(b)(1) is to maintain a consistent barrier height relative to the surface a person is standing on. For a sloped surface like a ramp, this means the measurement must be taken vertically from the ramp surface itself, resulting in a top rail that is parallel to the slope of the ramp.

questions.question: A safety net installation is complete. The Competent Person is preparing for the drop test. Which of the following conditions would invalidate the test before it even begins?
answers: The test is being conducted in the rain.
The sandbag to be used weighs 380 pounds.
The test is being conducted by the Competent Person and not a third party.
The net has a UV-resistant coating.
feedbacks: Incorrect: Weather conditions do not inherently invalidate the test, though they may affect safety.
Correct: 1926.502(c)(4)(i) strictly requires a 400-pound bag of sand. Using a lighter bag would not adequately test the net's shock-absorbing capacity.
Incorrect: The Competent Person is responsible for overseeing or conducting the test.
Incorrect: This is a desirable feature and does not invalidate the test.
questions.explanation: The drop test procedure outlined in 1926.502(c)(4)(i) is a prescriptive standard. It requires a 400-pound bag of sand with a diameter of roughly 30 inches. Using an underweight bag would not impart the required force to the system, and therefore a 'pass' would be meaningless. The installation would not be properly certified.

questions.question: As a Competent Person, you must ensure fall protection training is provided. According to 1926.503(a)(1), which of the following topics is NOT an explicitly required element of this training?
answers: The nature of fall hazards in the work area.
The correct procedures for erecting, maintaining, and disassembling fall protection systems.
The role of each employee in the safety monitoring system.
The specific brand names of all approved equipment.
feedbacks: Incorrect: This is explicitly required by 1926.503(a)(1)(i).
Incorrect: This is explicitly required by 1926.503(a)(1)(ii).
Incorrect: This is explicitly required by 1926.503(a)(1)(v).
Correct: Training must cover the types and use of equipment, but not specific brand names. The focus is on performance and compatibility, not marketing.
questions.explanation: OSHA 1926.503(a)(1) provides a detailed list of required training topics. The focus is on understanding hazards, procedures, limitations, and responsibilities. While employees must be trained on the specific equipment they will use, the standard does not mandate training on every possible brand name. The core requirement is competence with the systems in use, regardless of the manufacturer.

questions.question: During an inspection of a permanently installed vertical lifeline on a ladder, what THREE defects would require the system to be locked out of service immediately?
answers: The cable is lightly rusted but not pitted.
A broken wire is found in one strand of the wire rope.
The cable guides are bent, causing the cable to rub against the ladder rungs.
The tensioning spring at the bottom has lost its compression.
The manufacturer's data plate is faded but still legible.
The ladder rungs are painted safety yellow.
feedbacks: Incorrect: Light surface rust is generally acceptable if it can be cleaned and does not affect the cable's diameter or flexibility.
Correct: Any broken wires in a wire rope lifeline compromise its integrity and require immediate removal from service per manufacturer and ANSI standards.
Correct: Abrasion from rubbing on the structure can rapidly degrade the lifeline, so this represents an imminent failure risk.
Correct: Proper tension is critical for the function of the cable grab/sleeve. A loss of tension makes the system unreliable and unsafe.
Incorrect: As long as the critical information is legible, fading is not a removal criterion.
Incorrect: The condition of the ladder is a separate inspection; this does not affect the lifeline system's serviceability.
questions.explanation: A vertical lifeline system relies on all its components working in concert. A broken wire directly reduces the rope's breaking strength. A bent guide that causes abrasion creates a future failure point that must be corrected immediately. Improper tension can cause the fall arrester (cable grab) to fail to lock onto the cable during a fall. These are all critical failures per 1926.502(d)(21) and ANSI guidelines.

questions.question: A rescue must be performed from a permit-required confined space after a worker fell and is suspended inside. The on-site rescue plan, written by the Competent Person, fails to account for this. Why is this a major deficiency?
answers: The Competent Person is not authorized to write rescue plans for confined spaces.
It demonstrates a failure to anticipate foreseeable emergencies, combining fall and atmospheric hazards.
All confined space rescues must be performed by the local fire department.
The plan violates ANSI Z359, which prohibits vertical entry rescues.
feedbacks: Incorrect: A CP can write the plan, but it must be adequate and incorporate all hazards.

Correct: Rescue planning under 1926.502(d)(20) must account for the specific work environment. A fall into a PRCS is a complex, dual-hazard scenario requiring specialized procedures (e.g., air monitoring, retrieval systems) that a standard fall rescue plan would lack.
Incorrect: On-site teams can perform the rescue if properly trained and equipped.
Incorrect: ANSI Z359 provides guidelines for rescue, it does not prohibit vertical entry.
questions.explanation: This scenario highlights a failure in comprehensive hazard assessment, a key duty of the Competent Person. The rescue plan must be tailored to the specific situation. A fall rescue plan and a confined space rescue plan are not interchangeable. A worker suspended in a confined space may be exposed to toxic gases or an oxygen-deficient atmosphere, making the rescue far more complex and time-sensitive than a simple fall in open air.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference in purpose between a positioning system and a personal fall arrest system (PFAS)?
answers: Positioning systems use ropes, while PFAS use webbing.
A positioning system is designed to prevent a worker from reaching a fall hazard, while a PFAS arrests a fall that is already in progress.
Positioning systems only require a body belt, while PFAS requires a full-body harness.
A PFAS must limit arrest forces to 1,800 lbs, while a positioning system has no force limitations.
feedbacks: Incorrect: Both systems can use either ropes or webbing.

Correct: This is the core distinction. Positioning (also called restraint) keeps a worker in a safe area or supported, preventing any fall from occurring. Fall arrest activates only after a fall has begun.
Incorrect: While partially true (body belts can be used for positioning), the fundamental difference is function, not just components.
Incorrect: Positioning systems have their own strength requirements (e.g., 3,000 lbs anchorage) but are not designed for dynamic loading.
questions.explanation: This is a foundational concept for a Competent Person. A positioning system (per 1926.502(e)) supports a worker at a location, leaving their hands free, and is not designed to arrest a fall (e.g., rebar tying). A fall restraint system prevents the worker from reaching the fall hazard. A personal fall arrest system (PFAS) (per 1926.502(d)) does nothing until a fall occurs, at which point it is designed to safely stop the fall.

questions.question: A toeboard installed as part of a guardrail system must be a minimum of how high, and be able to withstand what force?
answers: 3.5 inches high; 50 pounds of force.
4 inches high; 100 pounds of force.
3 inches high; 25 pounds of force.
4.5 inches high; 50 pounds of force.
feedbacks: Correct: 1926.502(b)(13) and (j)(2) require toeboards to be a minimum of 3.5 inches in height and capable of withstanding a force of 50 pounds applied in any downward or outward direction.
Incorrect: The height and force requirements are lower than this.
Incorrect: The height and force requirements are higher than this.
Incorrect: The minimum height is 3.5 inches, not 4.5 inches.
questions.explanation: The specifications for toeboards are precise in Subpart M. The minimum 3.5-inch height (nominal lumber size of 2x4) is designed to prevent tools and materials from rolling off the edge. The 50-pound force requirement ensures it won't fail if struck by a sliding object or accidentally kicked. This is detailed in 1926.502(j).

questions.question: A competent person approves the use of a single, standard 6-foot shock-absorbing lanyard to be used as part of a horizontal lifeline between two stanchions. Why is this a critical error?
answers: The lanyard is too short to provide adequate mobility.
The lanyard's shock absorber is not designed for the increased fall forces of an HLL.
The snap hooks on the lanyard are not compatible with the stanchions.
The lanyard is not made of wire rope.
feedbacks: Incorrect: Mobility is not the life-safety issue here.

Correct: A fall on a flexible horizontal lifeline creates greater fall distances and higher arresting forces than a fall on a rigid anchor point. A standard lanyard's energy absorber may be insufficient or could fully deploy, transmitting excessive force to the worker.
Incorrect: While compatibility is important, the fundamental error is the misuse of the lanyard in this type of system.
Incorrect: Lanyards are typically made of webbing or synthetic rope, not wire rope.
questions.explanation: This is a common and deadly misconception. A horizontal lifeline (HLL) has sag, which increases both the fall distance and the forces generated during fall arrest. A standard personal energy absorber is calibrated for a fall on a rigid anchor. Using it on an HLL can lead to forces exceeding the 1,800 lb limit on the worker and can cause catastrophic system failure. Specialized HLL systems are required.

questions.question: Under what specific condition is it permissible to use a single 2x4 piece of lumber as a top rail for a guardrail system?
answers: When the posts are spaced no more than 6 feet apart.
When the '2-inch' dimension is oriented vertically, not horizontally.
When the wood is pressure-treated for outdoor use.
It is never permissible; two stacked 2x4s are always required.
feedbacks: Incorrect: Closer spacing helps, but is not the sole determining factor.

Correct: To utilize the full strength of the lumber, the 4-inch dimension should be vertical to resist downward force (like a floor joist). OSHA allows this if the wood is oriented to its stronger axis.
Incorrect: Treatment affects durability, not the structural strength needed to meet the 200 lb force test.
Incorrect: A single 2x4 can be compliant if it meets the performance test, which is much more likely when oriented correctly.
questions.explanation: OSHA's guardrail standard is performance-based. It must hold 200 lbs. While Appendix B to Subpart M provides examples (e.g., 2x4s), the key is meeting the performance requirement. A 2x4 laid flat is weak and will likely fail the 200 lb test. A 2x4 on its edge (with the 3.5" nominal dimension oriented vertically) is significantly stronger and more likely to meet the requirement, especially with appropriate post spacing. A competent person must understand this structural principle.

questions.question: A roofing contractor is using a safety monitoring system on a low-slope roof (4:12 pitch) with a width of 48 feet. According to 1926.502(h), what is the maximum number of workers a single safety monitor can be responsible for?
answers: 2 workers
4 workers
There is no specific limit, as long as the monitor can see them and is in communication.
The limit is one monitor per 50 feet of roof edge.
feedbacks: Incorrect: There is no limit of two workers.
Incorrect: There is no limit of four workers.

Correct: 1926.502(h)(1)(v) states the monitor shall be on the same level and within visual sighting distance and be able to communicate orally. It does not set a numerical limit, making it a judgment call for the competent person based on site conditions.
Incorrect: This is a misinterpretation of the rule that no worker shall be more than 50 feet from the monitor.
questions.explanation: The OSHA standard for safety monitors is performance-oriented. It requires the monitor to be able to see and hear the workers they are responsible for and to have no other distracting duties. It does not set a hard number (e.g., '6 workers'). The competent person must assess the specific site (roof size, obstructions, noise level) to determine how many workers one monitor can *effectively* and safely oversee at one time.

questions.question: During a harness inspection, the competent person finds that the fall arrest indicator, a patch of folded and stitched webbing, has been deployed. The worker claims he just 'snagged it on a nail' and didn't fall. What is the correct action?
answers: Ask the worker to sign a statement, then put the harness back in service.
Test the indicator by pulling on it to see if it deploys further.
Immediately remove the harness from service for disposal or recertification by the manufacturer.
Cut off the deployed indicator tag and continue to use the harness.
feedbacks: Incorrect: The physical evidence of the deployed indicator overrides the worker's statement.
